notes.title: Feature Importance across Domains for Improving Non-Intrusive Speech Intelligibility Prediction in Hearing Aids
notes.bp: A hearing-aid system needs an intelligibility estimate without asking a listener to score every noisy utterance.
notes.wh: Human scores are expensive, while acoustic features, learned representations, and hearing-aid conditions expose different parts of the perceptual problem.
notes.naive: Feed one feature family into a regressor and treat its error as a complete measure of intelligibility.
notes.ap: Estimate frame-level importance across spectral, temporal, and Whisper latent features, project each domain through those weights, and fuse them in an assessment model.
notes.mech: FiDo produces domain-specific weighted representations before concatenation and regression; RMSE on intelligibility targets evaluates whether the weighting preserves listener-relevant evidence.
notes.math: Feature selection is moved inside the representation: the model learns which moments and domains matter before the final proxy prediction.
notes.eval: Feature selection is moved inside the representation: the model learns which moments and domains matter before the final proxy prediction.
notes.ww: The paper reports that FiDo reduces MBI-Net+ RMSE from 26.10 to 24.11 and improves over the best 2023 Clarity Prediction Challenge system.
notes.limits: Weakly supervised targets, hearing-aid/noise conditions, challenge split, proxy RMSE, and absence of a new listener study bound the claim; prediction is not equivalent to real-world access improvement.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Prosodically Enhanced Foreign Accent Simulation by Discrete Token-based Resynthesis Only with Native Speech Corpora
notes.bp: Training and listening materials should expose learners and recognizers to foreign accents that are scarce in native-speech corpora.
notes.wh: Accent changes segmental realization and rhythm; a system that changes only discrete phonetic tokens can miss duration patterns characteristic of the speaker’s first language.
notes.naive: Use native speech unchanged or resynthesize token content without modeling timing, then call the result an accent simulation.
notes.ap: Add explicit duration modification to discrete-token resynthesis so native speech can approximate durational foreign-accent cues without accented training data.
notes.mech: Self-supervised discrete units preserve linguistic content, while duration controls alter timing before the units are rendered by a decoder; real L2 speech supplies the comparison target.
notes.math: Accent simulation is a structured transformation: content units should stay stable while temporal realization changes in a language-specific way.
notes.eval: Accent simulation is a structured transformation: content units should stay stable while temporal realization changes in a language-specific way.
notes.ww: The paper reports that the enhanced method reproduces durational accents observed in real L2 speech.
notes.limits: Accent languages, speakers, duration estimator, perceptual validation, and native-corpus assumptions bound transfer; acoustic similarity is not proof of improved ASR or pedagogy.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Diffusion Buffer: Online Diffusion-based Speech Enhancement with Sub-Second Latency
notes.bp: Live communication needs speech enhancement while the signal is still arriving, with latency small enough for interaction.
notes.wh: Diffusion models can restore complex distributions but normally require many iterative steps and future context, conflicting with streaming constraints.
notes.naive: Run an offline diffusion enhancer or use a fast deterministic model that sacrifices generative restoration quality.
notes.ap: Use a sliding buffer whose corruption schedule gives more noise to frames near the present, then denoise older frames with a controlled delay.
notes.mech: The buffer defines a causal-to-delayed window; diffusion steps operate on that window and output frames once their future context is sufficient.
notes.math: Latency becomes a tunable information budget: a larger buffer gives the score-based model more context while increasing input-output delay.
notes.eval: Latency becomes a tunable information budget: a larger buffer gives the score-based model more context while increasing input-output delay.
notes.ww: The paper reports better results than standard diffusion baselines and GPU input-output latency around 0.3–1 seconds.
notes.limits: GPU/hardware assumptions, buffer size, noise mixtures, real-time scheduling, and perceptual metrics bound the result; a reported latency range is not a full conversational user study.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Simultaneous Masked and Unmasked Decoding with Speculative Decoding Masking for Fast ASR without Accuracy Loss
notes.bp: An ASR decoder should approach autoregressive accuracy without paying for every sequential token decision.
notes.wh: Non-autoregressive guesses are fast but can lose accuracy, while autoregressive search repeatedly computes scores for hypotheses that are already predictable.
notes.naive: Choose either full autoregressive beam search or a non-autoregressive decoder and accept the speed-accuracy tradeoff.
notes.ap: Combine simultaneous masked/unmasked decoding with speculative masking so confidently predictable hypotheses skip unnecessary decoder computation.
notes.mech: Preliminary masked decisions identify positions whose score computation can be omitted; the remaining positions retain the autoregressive search path and its result.
notes.math: The method exploits conditional redundancy in sequence search: computation is spent where uncertainty remains rather than uniformly at every token.
notes.eval: The method exploits conditional redundancy in sequence search: computation is spent where uncertainty remains rather than uniformly at every token.
notes.ww: On TED-LIUM2, the paper reports WER 7.3% for both the proposed and autoregressive systems, with RTF 0.41 versus 0.59.
notes.limits: One corpus/model, beam and hardware settings, confidence thresholds, and real-time measurement protocol bound transfer; equal WER on one test set does not prove universal speed preservation.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: FlowTSE: Target Speaker Extraction with Flow Matching
notes.bp: A listener should extract one enrolled speaker from a mixture even when interference is severe or unseen.
notes.wh: Discriminative masks can create artifacts and fail under distribution shift, while generative pipelines often require multiple pretrained components and poor phase reconstruction.
notes.naive: Map the mixture directly to a mask or waveform with a large pipeline, ignoring the enrolled speaker’s distribution and phase evidence.
notes.ap: Condition flow matching on enrollment and mixture mel-spectrograms, and condition a vocoder on the mixture’s complex STFT when phase matters.
notes.mech: A learned flow transports a noisy conditional distribution toward target speech; complex-STFT conditioning supplies phase information that mel features discard.
notes.math: Target extraction is conditional generation under an identity constraint, with magnitude and phase treated as complementary evidence.
notes.eval: Target extraction is conditional generation under an identity constraint, with magnitude and phase treated as complementary evidence.
notes.ww: The paper reports that FlowTSE matches or outperforms strong target-speaker-extraction baselines on standard benchmarks.
notes.limits: Enrollment quality, speaker/noise shift, phase-vocoder design, benchmark mixtures, and signal metrics bound transfer; extraction quality is not automatically improved ASR or hearing-aid benefit.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Improving Noise Robustness of LLM-based Zero-shot TTS via Discrete Acoustic Token Denoising
notes.bp: Zero-shot TTS should preserve a speaker’s identity when the few-second audio prompt is noisy.
notes.wh: Noise corrupts acoustic tokens and can cause an LLM-based TTS system to copy the environment or plan the wrong voice, while ordinary enhancement may not match token-level prompts.
notes.naive: Enhance the prompt with a generic speech enhancer or trust the noisy codec tokens as if they represented clean speaker evidence.
notes.ap: Denoise the first acoustic-token groups with a neural codec token predictor, refine the embedding, and use the cleaned prompt in LauraTTS.
notes.mech: The token denoiser predicts clean coarse tokens; an embedding refiner and codec decoder reconstruct usable acoustic evidence before the zero-shot TTS model conditions generation.
notes.math: Denoising at the representation used for prompting aligns the cleanup objective with the generator’s actual conditioning interface.
notes.eval: Denoising at the representation used for prompting aligns the cleanup objective with the generator’s actual conditioning interface.
notes.ww: The paper reports that its codec denoiser outperforms speech-enhancement baselines and that noise-robust LauraTTS improves over adding an external enhancer.
notes.limits: Noise types, prompt duration, speaker overlap, codec/model version, and zero-shot evaluation bound transfer; clean synthesis from a prompt is not speaker-authenticated identity preservation.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Training-Free Voice Conversion with Factorized Optimal Transport
notes.bp: Any-to-any voice conversion should change identity from a short reference while preserving the source linguistic content, including across languages.
notes.wh: Nearest-neighbor replacement needs long reference recordings and can import language-specific artifacts; training a new converter per speaker defeats the any-to-any goal.
notes.naive: Replace each source embedding with its closest target embedding and assume five minutes of reference speech is always available.
notes.ap: Replace nearest-neighbor matching with a factorized optimal-transport map in WavLM embedding subspaces, requiring only a short reference.
notes.mech: Monge–Kantorovich linear transport aligns source and target feature distributions; factorization normalizes unequal variances before the encoder-converter-vocoder reconstructs speech.
notes.math: Optimal transport matches distributions rather than individual frames, allowing sparse reference evidence to define a target voice without storing a lookup for every source sound.
notes.eval: Optimal transport matches distributions rather than individual frames, allowing sparse reference evidence to define a target voice without storing a lookup for every source sound.
notes.ww: MKL-VC reports improved content preservation and short-reference robustness on LibriSpeech and FLEURS, with cross-lingual performance comparable to FACodec.
notes.limits: Reference duration, WavLM space, languages, vocoder, speaker similarity metric, and implementation choices bound transfer; content preservation does not prove perfect identity conversion.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: A Bayesian Approach to L2 Fluency Ratings by Native and Nonnative Listeners
notes.bp: Fluency ratings of second-language speech should reflect both the speaker’s temporal behavior and the listener’s linguistic background.
notes.wh: Listeners disagree, and native-listener norms may not transfer to nonnative listeners; rate, pauses, and repairs are correlated rather than independent cues.
notes.naive: Average all ratings or use a single syllable-rate predictor and treat the resulting score as a universal fluency scale.
notes.ap: Use a Bayesian hierarchical model to separate listener variability from utterance-level fluency cues and compare syllable- versus segment-based articulation rate.
notes.mech: Posterior distributions represent listener-specific leniency and cue weights; speed, breakdown, and repair features explain ratings while uncertainty remains explicit.
notes.math: Human evaluation is a multilevel measurement problem: the score is jointly produced by the speech sample and the observer’s perceptual prior.
notes.eval: Human evaluation is a multilevel measurement problem: the score is jointly produced by the speech sample and the observer’s perceptual prior.
notes.ww: Using 16 listeners and 180 Japanese speakers in J-AESOP, the paper reports greater leniency among some nonnative listeners and stronger fit for segment-based articulation rate.
notes.limits: Listener sample, language backgrounds, trained-rating task, corpus, feature definitions, and Bayesian priors bound transfer; fluency ratings are not a complete measure of communicative success.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
